newsitem.title: UK: CBI revises down UK 1997 growth forecasts.
newsitem.headline: CBI revises down UK 1997 growth forecasts.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said on Thursday it had revised down its forecast for economic growth in the UK to 2.8 percent from 3.1 percent previously, due to the strength of sterling.

The CBI also said it assumed that base rates in Britain would remain at 6.00 percent in the first half of 1997, before rising to 6.5 percent in the third quarter of this year, and then to 7.0 percent in 1998.
For underlying inflation, the CBI said it had revised its forecast down to 2.2 percent by the end of this year, compared with a previous forecast for 2.5 percent at end-1997.
"But it is expected to rise again to 2.7 percent by the end of 1998, compared with 2.9 percent in the previous forecast," the CBI said in a statement.
Output price inflation is expected to remain subdued throughout 1997, ending the year at 2.3 percent before rising to 2.8 percent by the end of 1998.

"While the overall economic outlook remains healthy, there is a less robust projection for the manufacturing sector as exports and profits growth come under pressure," Kate Barker, the CBI's chief economic advisor, said.
She said low inflation in the manufacturing sector would moderate inflationary prssures from rapid private consumption growth.
"We continue to expect that interest rates should only be increased modestly in 1997, but on present data a rate rise is not yes justified," Barker said.
The CBI said consumer spending is forecast to grow by 4.1 percent in 1997 and by a further 3.4 percent in 1998.

"This robust performance, which contributes the major part of overall GDP growth in 1997 and 1998, is due mainly to increases in disposable incomes and personal sector liquidity, including the effects of windfall gains," the CBI said.
It added that unemployment was expected to fall to 1.64 million by the end of 1997.
By end-1998, the number out of work is forecast to be at 1.59 million, while overall employment is expected to increase to almost 350,000 over the two years to the end of 1998.
